summary:
Dominica's High Court of Justice in Roseau struck sections 14 and 16 of the Sexual Offences Act on 23 April 2024, holding unconstitutional the provisions that criminalised consensual same-sex activity. The case was brought by a gay man living in Dominica (BBC, 23 Apr 2024; Human Rights Watch, 24 Apr 2024).

As a result of the ruling, consensual same-sex conduct between adults is no longer an offence under Dominica's Sexual Offences Act. The repeal came through judicial review of the statute rather than through an act of parliament: the High Court determined that the sections were unconstitutional.

The provisions had been under constitutional challenge before the 2024 ruling. MiRiDom founder Daryl Phillip announced a High Court challenge to Dominica's buggery and sexual-activity provisions at a news conference on 20 July 2019, five years before the provisions were struck down (Dominica News Online).

Dominica's documented diplomatic record includes signature of the 2011 Human Rights Council joint statement on ending acts of violence and related human rights violations based on sexual orientation and gender identity, whose signatory list includes 85 countries (US Mission Geneva, 22 Mar 2011). This is a dated commitment on the international record; it is not itself a domestic legal protection.

Local religious authority has publicly opposed criminalisation. Catholic Bishop Gabriel Malzaire of Dominica called in May 2013 for eliminating criminal penalties for homosexuality and for all forms of violence against LGBT people, citing the Holy See's position (Erasing 76 Crimes, 24 May 2013).

Regional context matters for planning: Human Rights Watch's April 2024 dispatch calls on all Caribbean nations to repeal comparable criminal laws, indicating that criminalising statutes remain in force elsewhere in the region. A visitor should not assume that the regime in Dominica is the regional norm.

Trans visitors face significant uncertainty. The sourced record addresses sexual-orientation criminalisation only. It does not document legal gender recognition rules, name or marker change procedures, anti-discrimination or hate-crime protections covering gender identity, access to trans-specific healthcare, or any documented pattern of anti-trans violence in Dominica.
tangentialFactors:
Decriminalisation in Dominica has been framed by outside advocacy bodies as part of a wider regional push. Human Rights Watch's dispatch of 24 April 2024 calls on all Caribbean nations to repeal comparable criminal laws, which means a visitor crossing into a neighbouring jurisdiction may face a materially different legal regime from the one now in force in Dominica itself.

The path to repeal was domestic litigation, not legislative reform: the High Court struck the Sexual Offences Act provisions as unconstitutional in April 2024, following a challenge filed in 2019 by MiRiDom founder Daryl Phillip. Advocacy framing treats the ruling as a milestone in an ongoing regional struggle for LGBT rights.

Dominica's 2011 signature of the Human Rights Council joint statement on violence based on sexual orientation and gender identity sits alongside 84 other countries, placing the territory in a documented international coalition on these issues. The statement's language covers gender identity as well as sexual orientation, but the signature does not translate into domestic legal provisions.

The 2013 statement by Catholic Bishop Gabriel Malzaire, who invoked the Holy See's position in calling for an end to criminal penalties and to violence against LGBT people, indicates that opposition to criminalisation was not solely a secular or international position in Dominica.
localsOnly:
The operative framework for residents is the ruling of the High Court of Justice: sections 14 and 16 of the Sexual Offences Act have been struck as unconstitutional, so the offences they created no longer apply. Enforcement questions after the ruling are governed by that judgment rather than by the text of the repealed sections.

The litigation that produced the ruling was initiated locally. MiRiDom founder Daryl Phillip filed the constitutional challenge in 2019 and announced it publicly at a news conference, which indicates an organised domestic advocacy presence behind the case.

On the religious-authority record, Catholic Bishop Gabriel Malzaire publicly called in May 2013 for an end to criminal penalties for homosexuality and for all forms of violence against LGBT people, invoking the Holy See's position. This is the only documented statement from local religious leadership contained in the inventory.

The inventory contains no source addressing how trans residents of Dominica obtain legal recognition of gender identity, change name or gender markers on civil documents, or access healthcare. Community-facing information on these matters is not available from the sources reviewed here.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Dominica's law provides legal gender recognition for trans people is unresolved. No source in the inventory addresses marker or name change procedures, or any process for updating birth certificates or identity documents to reflect a trans person's gender.

Whether Dominica's anti-discrimination provisions extend to gender identity, and whether its criminal law recognises offences motivated by gender identity as hate crimes, is not sourced here and remains unresolved.

No source in the inventory reports incidents of anti-trans violence in Dominica, and none addresses trans-specific healthcare access or the treatment of trans people in institutional settings. The absence of such reporting in the reviewed sources is not evidence that these risks are absent on the ground.

No source in the inventory documents how the former Sexual Offences Act provisions affected trans or gender-nonconforming people, including whether they could be used to compel psychiatric or medical intervention. This remains unverified.

A 2011 US State Department press statement relating to Dominica is cited in the inventory without its substance being reproduced; whether that statement addresses LGBT rights or other topics is unresolved.
